newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - Cockfighting all the fun of the Mexican fair.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cockfighting all the fun of the Mexican fair.

text.p: Rogelio Igartua chews a cigar, pours himself a generous measure of whisky and tucks betting slips under his felt cowboy hat for good luck.
He gives an approving glance as his handler deftly binds a razor blade to the back of a rooster's foot and anxiously waits for the next fight to begin.

Far from being a clandestine backalley activity, cockfighting draws capacity crowds all year round at fairs across Mexico such as the annual Easter horsefair held at Texcoco, 20 miles (30 km) northeast of Mexico City.
The cockpit is literally a star attraction, drawing some of Mexico's most highly sought entertainers, powerful politicians and crowds who barely blink at the flying feathers and bloodshed.

Top of the bill in Texcoco's cockpit recently was Mexico's most famous mariachi singer, Vicente Fernandez, resplendent in the traditional "charro," an elaborately embroidered cowboy outfit that has become his trademark. He is in his element here, evoking an idyllic bygone era when macho cowboys rode on horseback to cockfights held at ranches rather than getting stuck in smog-laden traffic in Mexico City.
The cockpit itself looks like a miniature version of the Mexican Stock Exchange, with runners carrying slips of paper and shouting prices beneath an electronic scoreboard and television screens.
A YUPPIE ATTRACTION?

In the line outside, yuppies dressed in immaculate denim look away from the Uzi-toting state troopers and accept free computer mouse pads with advertising slogans. Once inside, the outcome of the fight is almost a matter of pot-luck. There can be no betting on past form because roosters very rarely fight twice and one usually dies. Gamblers bet on the red or the green corner.

"Breeding counts, though. We do breed our own, but the best fighters come from Texas," Igartua, in the red corner, said. "If we keep winning then the odds come down. Right now we're paying ten-to-nine on."

A referee calls the handlers to order and they stroke the roosters' bright red, green and blue tail feathers and let their beaks touch, like boxers touching gloves. The bout then begins with a flurry of jabbing and pecking in mid-air to gain advantage before the roosters land and begin stabbing at each other on a blood-spattered floor.
The referee frequently decrees a 15-second break if the roosters become entangled, like boxers. During this time handlers may place their roosters' heads in their mouths.
"It's like mouth-to-mouth resuscitation," said Manuel Salinas, a country vet who follows the sport. "The roosters reach such a state of over-excitement they cannot breathe."
A rooster wins if he remains on the offensive after his opponent is immobile. Sometimes neither rooster can move and the fight is a draw if they remain that way for 15 minutes.
At the end of the fight handlers often tip their birds to pour the blood out of their beaks. In Texcoco, the moribund birds were left twitching on wooden racks outside the men's toilet.
NOT EVERYBODY IS PLEASED
Not everyone in Mexico is a fan. Writer and social commentator Carlos Monsivais says cockfighting is "obnoxious" and deserves the social stigma that has long made it illegal in other countries.

"Unfortunately, cruelty to animals is considered amusing in Mexico, like bullfighting," Monsivais told Reuters. "It's also a mixture of a show and gambling. There's no point in cockfighting without money," he said, noting that the fat wads of money changing hands bear testimony to this.
"What's more they humanise the roosters by strapping deadly weapons to them. It's like watching a knife fight."
Cruelty is not an issue for Mexico's many cockfighting enthusiasts.

"A breeder would say roosters are warriors and no warrior fears death," Salinas said. "It is true they often do not feel their wounds during the fight due to the adrenaline flowing, but they certainly do later. The animals then either die or are so badly maimed they have to be put down," he added. "A small few survive and are used to enrich the gene pool."
